name: Dienogest

lead: Dienogest is a prescription progestin best known as a standalone endometriosis treatment and as the progestin in several combined pills. Because it has antiandrogenic activity, some ethinylestradiol/dienogest pills are used or labelled for acne in women who also want contraception.
Evidence is stronger for endometriosis than for acne; no acne-specific trials were found among the sources reviewed.

paras: It activates the progesterone receptor and blocks the androgen receptor, suppressing ovulation and reducing androgen effects such as oiliness and acne, without androgenic activity of its own.

Reported effects include irregular bleeding, headache, nausea, breast tenderness, mood changes and weight gain. Combined pills carry a boxed warning for smokers over 35 and an increased clot risk; long-term use may lower bone density. Prescription-only.

lead: Dienogest is a synthetic progestin derived from 19-nortestosterone, developed by Bayer's predecessor companies. It is used as a 2 mg standalone treatment for endometriosis in many countries and as the progestin in several combined oral contraceptives and menopausal products.[1][2] It is sometimes called a fourth-generation progestin.[1]

Dienogest differs from many 19-nortestosterone progestins in that it is described as having antiandrogenic rather than androgenic activity, and this is the basis for its interest in acne.[1][2] Wikipedia notes that acne is not a listed indication for standalone dienogest but that an estradiol valerate/dienogest product was in registration in Europe for acne, while Grokipedia states that ethinylestradiol/dienogest combinations are approved in the European Union for moderate acne in women who choose oral contraception and for whom topical treatment or antibiotics failed.[1][2]
Combined products carry the standard combined-pill boxed warning about smoking and cardiovascular events.[3]
infobox: Prescription-only; not available as a standalone drug in the US or UK

paras: Dienogest appears in the appearance context through combined pills used for acne in women who also want contraception. According to Grokipedia, ethinylestradiol/dienogest products are approved in the EU for moderate acne under these circumstances, and its antiandrogenic activity is cited as the reason it may help androgen-dependent symptoms.[2] Wikipedia describes acne as not being a listed indication and mentions an estradiol valerate/dienogest combination in European pre-registration for acne.[1] Because these accounts differ, the exact regulatory status of acne indications may vary by product and country.

The main use of 2 mg dienogest is endometriosis-associated pelvic pain, approved in Japan in 2007 and Europe in 2009 and since in many other countries.[1][2] It is also used in contraceptive pills with ethinylestradiol (for example Valette) or estradiol valerate (Natazia, Qlaira), for heavy menstrual bleeding in the Natazia product in the US, and in some menopausal products.[1][3]

Wikipedia lists menstrual irregularities, headache, nausea, breast tenderness, depression, acne, weight gain and flatulence as common effects.[1] Contraindications include active venous thromboembolism, cardiovascular disease and hormone-dependent cancers such as breast cancer.[1] Combinations with estradiol valerate are associated with increased venous thromboembolism risk, described as lower than for ethinylestradiol-based pills.[1]

Grokipedia notes that long-term progestin therapy may reduce bone mineral density, and that bone health monitoring is advised during extended treatment.[2] The US Natazia label carries the combined-pill boxed warning for smokers over 35, and lists liver disease and high blood pressure among warnings.[3]

Dienogest is a progesterone receptor agonist with antiandrogenic activity and no reported estrogenic, glucocorticoid or mineralocorticoid activity.[1] Reviews of progestin pharmacology describe how structural differences among progestins change their receptor profiles.[4][5] It suppresses ovulation mainly through a direct ovarian action and has direct antiproliferative effects on endometriotic lesions.[1][2] Studies of four oral contraceptives compared effects on sex hormones and binding globulins.[6]

Oral bioavailability is about 90 percent and the elimination half-life roughly 7.5 to 10.7 hours; it is metabolised mainly by CYP3A4, so ketoconazole and erythromycin can raise exposure and rifampicin can lower it.[1][2]

Dienogest was synthesised in 1979 in Jena, Germany, under the code STS-557, and first marketed in 1995 in the Valette combined pill.[1] Dinagest launched in Japan in 2007 for endometriosis, Visanne followed in Europe in 2009 and Australia in 2010, and the estradiol valerate/dienogest pills Natazia and Qlaira were introduced in 2009-2010.[1]

Brand names include Visanne, Dinagest and Alondra (endometriosis), Valette, Natazia, Qlaira and Klaira (contraception), and Climodien (menopause).[1] It is prescription-only; it is Schedule 4 in Australia and is not available as a standalone medication in the US or UK.[1] No community discussion sources were reviewed for this entry.

The best-documented trial evidence concerns endometriosis. A 24-week randomized, open-label non-inferiority trial found dienogest as effective as leuprolide acetate for endometriosis-related pain.[7] Reviews describe progesterone resistance in endometriosis and hormonal treatment options, and dienogest has also been reviewed for adenomyosis.[8][9][10] Registered trials include studies in adenomyosis, ovarian endometrioma, comparisons with goserelin and danazol, and a real-world study in Indian women.[11][12][13][14]
No trial among the sources reviewed tested dienogest specifically for acne as a primary outcome; acne indications for combined pills rest on the product labelling described above.
